Sucka
SUK-uh
noun / interjection (Gen X slang)
The Black American pronunciation of sucker, which in 19th-century American English meant a dupe, a greenhorn, an easy mark (probably from sucker, a young animal not yet weaned). Sucka was at home in African-American speech and 1970s film long before it went national, and the Keenen Ivory Wayans comedy I’m Gonna Git You Sucka (1988) affectionately parodied the films that had used it. It became a household taunt through Mr. T, whose B. A. Baracus on NBC’s The A-Team (1983–87) growled sucka and fool at the villains every week, a year after his Clubber Lang in Rocky III (1982) gave the country "I pity the fool."

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sucka is the playground word for a dupe: the kid who fell for the trick, the mark who paid too much, the bad guy who walked straight into the A-Team’s trap. When Mr. T growled it at a villain, it meant "you got played, and you had it coming." The word carries two things at once: a warning against being gullible and a sneer at those who are. Scripture keeps the warning and refuses the sneer. Proverbs has its own word for the sucka: the simple. "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15); "A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished" (Pro 22:3). Paul warns of men who "by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple" (Rom 16:18), and he wants believers to be "no more children, tossed to and fro" by the sleight of men (Eph 4:14). Our Lord sends His disciples out "wise as serpents, and harmless as doves" (Mat 10:16) — not easy marks, and not con men either. But the same Lord forbids the contempt: "whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire" (Mat 5:22). Wisdom calls the simple to come and learn (Pro 1:22); she does not mock them. A father can tell his son: don’t be a sucka — test what you hear, read the fine print, and know the Word well enough to spot a counterfeit. And when you see another boy get played, don’t sneer. Help him up; you were simple once too.

Webster 1828 Definition

Black American pronunciation of sucker (a dupe, an easy mark), made a national taunt by Mr. T on The A-Team (1983); Scripture warns against being the simple who believeth every word (Pro 14:15) but forbids the sneer of "Thou fool" (Mat 5:22).

SUCKA, n. and interj. (Gen X slang, 1970s–80s, African-American speech; national via The A-Team, 1983) A dupe, a chump, an easy mark; a taunt thrown at a beaten opponent. "You just got played, sucka."

From American sucker, a greenhorn or dupe (19th c.); compare sucker punch; the dropped -r reflects Black American pronunciation.

Companion taunts: fool, chump; Mr. T’s "I pity the fool" (Rocky III, 1982); parodied in I’m Gonna Git You Sucka (1988).

Webster 1828: SUCKER, n. He or that which draws with the mouth. …

Decode for parents: the word warns against being gullible and sneers at the gullible; keep the warning, drop the sneer.

Key Scripture

Pro 14:15 — "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going."

Pro 22:3 — "A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished."

Rom 16:18 — "For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple."

Mat 10:16 — "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves."

Mat 5:22 — "But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire."

Modern Corruption

Sucka rightly warns against being easily played but turns the warning into contempt; Scripture calls the simple to wisdom and forbids the man who says, Thou fool.

expand to see more

Contempt for the conned. In the world of the taunt, the con man is clever and the mark is a loser — the blame quietly slides from the deceiver to the deceived. Scripture never makes that move. Paul denounces the men who "deceive the hearts of the simple" (Rom 16:18); he does not laugh at the simple. A boy raised on sucka can learn to admire the hustle and despise the hustled, and that is exactly backwards. Our Lord set a guard over the mouth: "Thou fool," spoken in contempt, is a matter for judgment (Mat 5:22).

Wise, not cynical. The cure for gullibility is not cynicism but prudence. The prudent man "looketh well to his going" (Pro 14:15) and "foreseeth the evil" (Pro 22:3); the believer is "wise as serpents, and harmless as doves" (Mat 10:16). A Christian ought to be the hardest man in the room to con — because he knows the Word, counts the cost, and is not hungry for the easy deal — and the gentlest man in the room toward the one who got conned. Wisdom stands in the street and calls the simple home (Pro 1:22).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English sucan (to suck) → sucker, an unweaned young animal → 19th-c. American sucker (a dupe) → Black American sucka → Mr. T, The A-Team (1983); Scripture: the simple believeth every word (Pro 14:15).

"Don’t be the mark, and don’t mock the mark (Mat 5:22)."
